ARTICLE IN PRESS Job-housing balance and job burnout among migrant workers: Mechanisms and implications for housing support policies Wei wanqing1,2& Li linyu1 Abstract Previous studies have examined the supply of housing support and the economic impact of job-housing separation. However, they have paid inadequate attention to the location selection of affordable housing with a job-housing balance and its effects on migrant workers' job burnout. To examine the effects and mechanisms of the job-housing balance in affordable housing locations on job burnout, this study employs the latest 2018 China Labour Force Dynamic Survey data and in-depth interview data on housing support for migrant workers collected by our research team in 2023. Our findings indicate that the job-housing balance significantly reduces job burnout, with this effect being more pronounced in the manufacturing sector and other industries. Labour intensity masks the impact of job-housing balance on job burnout, whereas work quality fully mediates this relationship exclusively in dormitory-type arrangements. This study offers policy implications for optimizing the siting of housing support projects. It also enhances the living conditionsS of affordable housing and promotes integrated urban-rural development. S E Keywords: Housing support; Job-housing balance; Migrant workers; Job burnout. R P 1. Introduction Housing security plays a vital role in urban–rural iNntegration. Since the 20th National Congress, the Chinese government has significantly increased the construction and supply of subsidized housing. In addition, it has I refined the dual-track housing supply system, com bining market-driven and government-supported approaches. Previous studies focus on housing support andE affordability (Hu & Qian, 2017; Wang, 2000; Zeng et al., 2019; Afshan & Sinha, 2023) but pay insufficieLnt attention to site selection and optimization. In reality, migrant workers' housing choices, influenced bCy payment capacity and transportation resources, demonstrate a balance between meeting residential needs and fulfilling employment demands, reflecting a job-housing balance (Li & I Zhao, 2022; Zhao et al., 2020; Fernandez & Su, 2004). However, affordable housing is often located outside of T cities (You et al., 2015) and far from workplaces, resulting in higher commuting costs. This spatial mismatch R affects residents' quality of life and their performance at work, as well as triggering the phenomenon of "affordable housing abanAdonment," which hampers migrant workers' integration into the city. As a result, optimizing the location of affordable housing on the basis of job-housing balance principles is critical for ensuring housing security and promoting integrated urban-rural development. Housing location choices have a relatively strong impact on employment among low-income groups. The literature has shown that mismatched residential and employment locations negatively impact traditional economic indicators, such as job opportunities and income returns (Kain, 1968; 1992; Hu & Wang, 2019). From the perspective of commuting time costs, relevant studies have explained how housing location choices affect work efficiency, job commitment, and mental health (Xiao et al., 2021; Chatterjee et al., 2020). Previous studies have not paid sufficient attention to the job‒housing balance of housing location models that are popular among migrant workers. Moreover, no theoretical analysis or empirical study linking affordable housing location with job burnout has been conducted. Thus, this study focuses on optimizing site selection within the housing security system. We examine the impact of job-housing balance on affordable housing location decisions and job burnout. To address the challenge of directly observing the social effects of the job-housing balance, this study focuses on labour dormitories as a typical practice of work–residence balance. In addition, we introduce a metric for assessing the job‒housing balance on the basis of commute time. Using data from the China Labour Force Dynamics Survey of 2018 and in-depth interviews with migrant workers in 2023, the study empirically analyses the effects of job- 1 School of Public Policy and Management, Guangxi University, Nanning, China. 2School of Social Development, East China  Normal University, Shanghai, China. e-mail: 1158626345@qq.com ARTICLE IN PRESS housing balance and housing location on job burnout and its underlying mechanisms. The main findings of this study are as follows. First, job-housing balance-oriented affordable housing locations significantly alleviate job burnout, with this effect being more pronounced among migrant workers in manufacturing and other industries. Second, the alignment of affordable housing locations with a job-housing balance effectively reduces job burnout by enhancing job quality. However, increased labour intensity weakens its alleviating effect on job burnout. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews studies on the relationship between housing location and job burnout and proposes research hypotheses on the basis of this review. Section 3 introduces the data, variables, and methods, and Section 4 presents the results of the main hypothesis tests and their interpretations. Section 5 presents the conclusion and discussion. 2. Literature Review and Research Hypotheses 2.1 Literature Review With respect to the impact of housing location on job burnout, previous studies have focused on the impact of commuting time on workplace burnout. This has led to the development of two explanation pathways. The first framework conceptualizes commuting time as a stressogenic factor. Empirical studies have indicated that prolonged commuting duration significantly increases employees' anxiety levels and exacerbates psychological distress and fatigue (Hansson et al., 2011), ultimately decreasing workpSlace performance through increased absenteeism, reduced task efficiency, and impaired concentration (Novaco & Gonzalez, 2009; Xiao et al., 2021; S De et al., 2022). Furthermore, the encroachment of lengthy commutes on leisure and family time intensifies E work-family conflict, thereby transmuting commuting stress into job burnout (Shen et al., 2021; Denstadli et al., 2017). Notably, women—who are disproportionately responsRible for household caregiving duties—exhibit heightened vulnerability to commuting-induced burnout (ClaPrk et al., 2020). The second framework emphasizes the stress-buffering function of commuting time. Commu ting establishes a "transitional buffer zone" between professional and domestic spheres (Pindek et al., 2023)N, offering opportunities for psychological detachment and cognitive recovery (Olsson et al., 2013; Redmond & Mokhtarian, 2001). This transitional period not only I facilitates mental preparation for work deman ds (Jachimowicz et al., 2020) but also enables postwork recuperation to enhance family engagement E(Jain & Lyons, 2008). In particular, individuals adopting short- distance or active commuting modes (e.g.L, walking/cycling) demonstrate better mental health outcomes and greater work engagement (Ma & Ye, 20C19; Friman et al., 2017; Chatterjee et al., 2020). 2.2 Brief Comments and Research Hypotheses I Overall, the literature on the impact of commuting time costs on job burnout is substantial. However, T previous studies have focused on job‒housing spatial mismatch but have paid insufficient attention to the R practical job-housing balance strategy frequently adopted by migrant workers. Moreover, previous studies have focused primarily on dimAensions related to job burnout, such as mental health, work efficiency, and job engagement. However, job burnout itself receives little direct attention. Therefore, the relationship between affordable housing location and job burnout remains underexplored. To address this gap, this paper adopts a job- housing balance perspective to analyse how the location selection of affordable housing affects job burnout among migrant workers. This study aims to provide substantial empirical evidence for research on housing support. This study is based on Demerouti et al.’s (2001) job demand-resources (JD-R) model. Affordable housing in which job-housing is balanced could be regarded as a structural job resource that not only improves work motivation but also partially mitigates the negative effects of high job demand. Specifically, this spatial alignment between housing and employment opportunities reduces transportation cost burdens disproportionately, affecting low-income households. Job-housing balanced housing achieves dual benefits. Productivity gains via minimized commuting costs (Zhao & Hu, 2019), mental health improvements through stress reduction (Friman et al., 2017), and quality-of-life enhancement (Olsson et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2011). Critically, such housing further lowers living expenses while balancing affordable spatial needs with employment accessibility. This dual cost reduction mechanism leads to a reduction in burnout symptoms. Hypotheses 1 is therefore proposed. Hypothesis 1. The job-housing balance can significantly mitigate job burnout. Furthermore, on the basis of the job demand-resources (JD-R) model, this study derives the mechanism through which job-housing balanced affordable housing alleviates job burnout. From a job demands perspective, job-housing balanced housing may paradoxically increase labour time ARTICLE IN PRESS and intensity. First, spatial proximity to workplaces reduces commuting time, incentivizing low-income employees to convert saved time into earnings over time (Zhang et al., 2023a; Dong et al., 2018). Second, employer-provided integrated housing blurs job-housing boundaries, exposing employees to employer-mediated residential control that coerces extended working hours (Jones et al., 2024). Over time, burnout risks increase through psychological attrition and social depletion. Studies have shown that chronic overwork is correlated with depression, anxiety, and diminished motivation (Choi et al., 2021; Chireh et al., 2023). Moreover, excessive labour crowds out familial and recreational time, exacerbating work-family conflicts (Gong, 2023; Tsutsumi, 2019). Conversely, job-housing balanced affordable housing counteracts these effects by housing security externalities. By decoupling residential access from employment status, such housing buffers against exploitative labour practices while maintaining spatial efficiency (Zhang et al., 2023b). On this basis, this study proposes Hypothesis 2a. Hypothesis 2a. Labour intensity mediates the relationship between job-housing balanced affordable housing and job burnout, resulting in a "suppressing effect". From the perspective of job resources, job-housing balanced affordable housing constitutes a critical employee welfare mechanism. This integration enhances work quality (Hong et al., 1995) and mitigates job burnout (Ashrafi et al., 2018). Specifically, it reduces average commute time and improves job satisfaction (Liu & Ma, 2024). Moreover, it lowers voluntary turnover risk among low-inScome workers through housing cost subsidies (Smith, 2003). The increase in housing security, work quality, and other work resources brought about S by the integration of work and housing guarantee housing can help promote work engagement and reduce job burnout. On this basis, the study proposes Hypothesis 2b. E Hypothesis 2b. Work quality mediates the relationship beRtween job-housing balanced affordable housing and job burnout. The data were obtained from the 2018 China Labour Force C Dynamic Survey (CLDS) administered by the Sun Yat-sen University Social Science Survey Center in 2019. The data were collected across 29 prIovinces, municipalities, and autonomous regions throughout China (except T for Hong Kong, Macao, Taiwan, Tibet, and Hainan), among the urban and rural workforce aged 15 to 64. These data include information on Rindividuals' gender, age, years of education, workplace characteristics, income, social capital, and job burnout. A notable strength of this dataset is its inclusion of information on residential A typology variables, particularly employer-provided dormitories, as a job-housing balance model, which effectively mitigates commuting cost distortions in labour market analysis. For our purposes, employed individuals aged 16–65 were selected as the study subjects. Observations with missing values for the relevant variables were eliminated, resulting in a valid sample of 2,758. Within this cohort, 482 employees resided in dormitory-style job-housing balanced accommodations, and 1,076 employed nondormitory job-housing balanced accommodations, collectively representing 56.5% of the total sample. Second, regional in-depth interview data were used. In 2023, the research team conducted semistructured interviews with 12 migrant workers aged 30–55 in the Pearl River Delta (PRD) region, focusing on postpandemic residential choices, job stability, and policy perceptions. The PRD was selected because of its dual representativeness. Since the PRD is China’s economic frontier and a global manufacturing hub, more than half of the migrant workers in this region reside in employer-provided dormitories during their early employment stages (Wei & Zhang, 2024). This phenomenon creates a natural laboratory for examining the socioeconomic impacts of job-housing balance patterns. Furthermore, the region’s housing policy outcomes demonstrate significant external validity, offering transferable insights for other newly industrialized regions. Additionally, the temporal window of these interviews captures the interactive dynamics between postpandemic housing policy adjustments and labour market restructuring. Methodologically, the interview data are triangulated with the China Labour Force Dynamic Survey (CLDS), enabling simultaneous macrolevel trend analysis and microlevel mechanism interpretation. 3.2 Variables ARTICLE IN PRESS 3.2.1 Dependent Variable Job burnout is defined as a psychological syndrome arising from chronic workplace stress and comprises three core dimensions: emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and reduced self-efficacy (Maslach et al., 2001). Four items adapted from the Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI) were used to measure job burnout. As a measure of emotional exhaustion, participants answered the following questions: "Work makes me feel physically and mentally exhausted," and "Working all day is very stressful for me" (scale: never=1; a few times a year =2; a few times a month=3; a few times a week=4; daily=5). Depersonalization was measured as follows: "I am increasingly indifferent to my job" (scale: never=1, a few times a year =2, a few times a month=3, a few times a week=4, daily=5). Reduced personal accomplishment was evaluated as follows: "I feel that I have accomplished a great deal of valuable work" (reverse-coded: never=5, a few times a year =4, a few times a month=3, a few times a week=2, daily=1). Scores were summed across all items to create a composite burnout severity index, where higher values indicate stronger burnout manifestation. 3.2.2 Core Independent and Mediation Variables This study focuses on the impact of job–housing balance-oriented affordable housing locations on job burnout, providing a basis for optimizing affordable housing site selection. The core independent variable is the location of job-housing balance-oriented affordable housing. Given that affordable housing projects often face high abandonment rates because locations are distant from workplaces, direSctly observing the effects of different locations presents challenges. Therefore, this paper selects a practical institutional pattern that effectively S achieves job-housing balance—labour dormitories—as a key entry point. Unlike the spontaneous and disorderly E slum settlements found in countries such as Brazil and India, China's labour dormitories embody a system in which production and living spaces are highly integrated undRer capital-driven arrangements, representing a typical pattern for the job-housing balance (Ren, 2018). HowPever, while the labour dormitory is a representative indicator, it struggles to fully capture the complexity and dynamic nature of the job-housing relationship. To more accurately measure job-housing balance, this Npaper introduces a commuting time-based job-housing balance metric in addition to labour dormitory occupancy status. The specific operationalization method is as I follows: Labour dormitories. With respect to the sEurvey item “Does your employer provide accommodations?”, the variable is coded 1 if the answer is yes, indicating residence in a labour dormitory. If the answer is no, the value L is coded 0, indicating residence outside the labour dormitories. A dormitory-based job-housing balance support C pattern is identified by this variable. I Job-Housing Balance Level: A four-category ordinal variable is constructed based on labour dormitory T occupancy status and commute time. Specifically, labour dormitories are highly job-housing balanced and valued at 4. Not living in labour doRrmitories and with a commute time of less than 20 minutes is considered a job- housing balance and is asAsigned a value of 3. Not residing in labour dormitories and having a commute time between 20 and 40 minutes is considered job-housing separation and is assigned a value of 2. Not residing in labour dormitories and having a commute time of more than 40 minutes is considered severe job-housing separation and is assigned a value of 1. According to Hypotheses 2a and 2b, job-housing balanced affordable housing primarily reduces job burnout through labour intensity masking effects and work quality alleviation mechanisms. Specifically, the spatiotemporal proximity between such housing and workplaces increases labour intensity, which subsequently leads to job burnout through heightened job demands. However, the extrinsic incentive effects of housing assistance partially counteract this burnout. Conversely, job-housing balance enhances work-related resources, including employment benefits, housing subsidies, and job quality improvements, thereby mitigating burnout risk. Consequently, this study operationalizes labour intensity and work quality as mediating variables, with the measurement protocols detailed below. Labour intensity: Operationalized through the survey item “How many hours do you typically work weekly at your current/most recent job?” Following Article 36 of China's Labour Contract Law, which mandates ≤44- hour standard workweek, this study classifies working more than 45 hours per week as “high labour intensity”, which is dichotomously coded as 1. Otherwise, the variable is coded 0. Work quality is measured using workers' overall job satisfaction with their current/last position. Responses were captured via a five-point Likert-type scale: very dissatisfied, somewhat dissatisfied, neutral, somewhat satisfied, and very satisfied, anchored from 1 (very dissatisfied) to 5 (very satisfied). Higher scores correspond to more positive work quality evaluations. Parenthetical standard errors are robust. Since the abovementioned methods can only partially alleviate the endogeneity issue, this study introduces the instrumental variables approach (IV). There are two IVs selected at the urban level: the occupancy rate of labour dormitories and the prevalence of job-housing balance. The rationale for IV selection is twofold. Relevance: Both reflect regional labour residential preferences, directly shaping individual housing location choices. Exogeneity: Both are driven by exogenous policy factors (e.g., municipal investment incentives, mixed- use zoning, and transit network density). Individual job-housing decisions cannot alter regional job-housing patterns in the short term. Thus, IVs are not directly related to job burnout. As the number of IVs equals the number of endogenous variables, this constitutes an exact identification. Exogeneity cannot be directly tested statistically at present. A qualitative discussion is the only way to proceed. Several factors may influence job burnout through potential pathways, such as urban infrastructure adequacy, public service accessibility, and urban social support systems. First, the instrumental variables are not significantly correlated with urban infrastructure development. Urban infrastructure development is not the sole determinant of job burnout. Job burnout is frequently attributed to high workloads and repetitive tasks (Ward et al., 2021). Second, migrant workers' urban-level job-housing status primarily reflects survival strategy adaptation rather than institutionalized social support. These findings collectively validate the theoretical plausibility of the instrumental variables within the exact identification framework. Conclusion and Discussion Affordable housing location plays an important role in influencing migrant workers' livelihoods and employment. In addition, it accelerates urban integration and urban–rural convergence. This study uses the 2018 China Labour Force Dynamics Survey (CLDS) dataset and 2023 in-depth interviews with migrant workers in the Pearl River Delta region (conducted by the research team) to analyse how job-housing balanced affordable housing locations impact job burnout. The following conclusions are drawn from this study. First, job-housing balanced affordable housing can significantly reduce job burnout, and the robustness test also supports this conclusion. Second, from the perspective of industry differences, the inhibitory effect of job-housing balanced affordable housing on job burnout is more pronounced in manufacturing and other industries. Finally, further mechanism tests reveal that labour intensity plays a masking role in the influence of job-housing balanced affordable housing on work burnout, whereas job quality functions solely as a complete mediator of the effect of dormitory-type job-housing balanced affordable housing on job burnout. The interview data further validate the aforementioned mechanisms. The mitigating effect of job-housing balanced affordable housing locations on job burnout in the Pearl River Delta region exhibits both nationwide applicability and distinct regional characteristics. As China is an economic frontier and a global manufacturing hub, the industrial structure of the Pearl River Delta has a particularly pronounced effect on alleviating the impact of job-housing balanced ARTICLE IN PRESS affordable housing locations in the manufacturing sector. This study explores the relationship between job-housing balanced affordable housing locations and job burnout. The academic community has similar concerns about labour mobility and informal housing in the context of globalization. Transnational research consistently acknowledges the importance of housing support for mobile workers' job stability and well-being (Sassen, 2018). This study reveals that the key role of job- housing balanced affordable housing location decisions in alleviating job burnout is empirically supported in developing countries. Poor transportation accessibility in Indian slums and Nairobi, Kenya, inhibits productivity and economic opportunities for lower- and middle-income groups (Jana et al., 2016; Nakamura & Avner, 2021). A job-housing balance is illustrated from the opposite perspective. Moreover, informal communities in Santiago, Chile, have enhanced residents' life satisfaction by shortening commutes and strengthening mutual support networks (Celhay & Gil, 2020). These cases collectively demonstrate the universal value of optimizing housing locations to improve the job-housing balance for workers. This paper offers significant implications for refining China's housing support and labour policy-making. Housing support policies should be focused not only on the construction and supply of affordable housing but also on the optimal location of affordable housing. Integrating job-housing balance considerations into housing support policy design holds urgent practical significance. To mitigate job burnout and ensure workers' sustainable employment, labour policies should strengthen oversight oSver excessive working hours. The following are specific policy recommendations. S First, the construction and supply of affordable housing should be increased to help migrant workers balance the cost of housing and commuting. Job-housing balanced affordableE housing not only aligns with the residential space selection logic of migrant workers in balancing housing anRd commuting costs but also effectively satisfies their dual demands for living space and employment quality during urban integration. Therefore, local P governments can proceed with the housing needs of vulnerable groups. Building according to demand is based on local economic capabilities and real estate market cNonditions. When determining the locations for affordable housing, priority should be given to areas with convenient transportation and comprehensive public facilities to I promote job-housing balance. Preference should be given to constructing job-housing balanced affordable housing in the vicinity of key industry sites inE urban development, particularly in the manufacturing and other sectors. Additionally, governments can purchase existing housing such as vacant labour dormitories and convert L them into dormitory-type affordable rental housing to compensate for the inadequate supply of job-housing C balanced affordable housing. Second, a targeted housing subIsidy policy should be implemented to reduce the burden of job-housing T balance housing on migrant workers. Currently, job-housing balanced affordable housing is notably lacking, so numerous migrant workers hRave to rely on the market to address their housing difficulties. However, market- supplied job-housing balanced housing still poses considerable economic pressure. Consequently, local A governments can provide tiered housing rental subsidies to eligible housing-challenged groups on the basis of the average rental levels in different cities and regions and the income levels of migrant workers. The provision of housing rental subsidies can enhance the rental payment capacity of these housing-challenged groups and revitalize existing housing stock, such as "industrial-to-residential conversions," "commercial-to-residential conversions," and urban villages, thereby effectively increasing the supply of job-housing balanced affordable rental housing. Furthermore, to ensure the effective utilization of housing rental subsidies, subsidies should be paid directly to property owners. Third, public service infrastructure should be improved to address migrant workers' diverse and multilevel housing needs. In this new era, the housing security needs of agricultural migrant populations extend beyond mere low-cost living spaces; instead, diversified needs such as job-housing balance, contentment in work and life, family reunification, children's education, and medical services have become increasingly prominent. However, job-housing balanced housing is located in urban villages, construction sites, labour dormitories, and shack settlements, where low-income agricultural migrant populations tend to concentrate and often suffer from poor living environments, inadequate supporting facilities, and low levels of public service provision. Therefore, local governments should align with the needs of low-income agricultural migrant populations by enhancing the construction of supporting facilities and improving the level of public service provision to increase the quality of job-housing balanced affordable housing. On the one hand, strengthening the development of urban integrated transportation systems that are more sensitive to the needs of low-income agricultural migrant populations is imperative. While prioritizing highways and urban rail transit systems, the practical needs of low-income ARTICLE IN PRESS agricultural migrant populations should be integrated into transportation planning to enhance commuting efficiency. On the other hand, efforts should be intensified to improve the community environment of job- housing balanced affordable housing. This not only involves providing public service facilities such as culture, sports, and public health that are commensurate with the growing number of low-income agricultural migrant people but also ensuring that those residing in job-housing balanced affordable housing enjoy urban benefits related to housing, including residence registration, children's education, and social security, thereby achieving equitable housing. This study has four key limitations. First, the geographical scope of the interview samples is constrained to residents of informal settlements in China's Pearl River Delta. Geographic bias inherent in this sampling may limit the generalizability of the conclusions, necessitating cross-regional comparisons (e.g., Yangtze River Delta vs. Northeast Rust Belt) for theoretical validation. Second, regarding data constraints, both the national tracking survey and regional interview data are cross-sectional. Unobserved confounders—including regional cultural norms (e.g., Guangdong's Lingnan culture) and urban governance characteristics—may violate the exclusion restriction assumptions of instrumental variables. Future research will employ panel data to rigorously construct instruments that strengthen causal identification. Third, the operationalization of housing typologies currently relies on employer-provided dormitories and commute duration thresholds. This framework lacks granularity regarding housing quality indices and community service accessibiliSty and fails to fully capture the multidimensional housing deprivation profiles characteristic of low-income migrant populations. Future follow- S up survey data collected by the research group will incorporate these indicators. Fourth, the analysis of mediating pathways is still incomplete. While this study focuses on labour intenEsity suppression and work quality buffering, other plausible mechanisms need to be explored. Moreover, fuRture research should test additional mediating variables. JSON: Name: job_housing_burnout_pipeline Title: Causal mediation and instrumental-variable analysis of job-housing balance effects on job burnout among migrant workers Short Hypothesis: Provision of job-housing balanced housing (measured by employer-provided dormitory residence or commute time ≤20 minutes) causally reduces job burnout scores among migrant workers relative to non-balanced housing, controlling for individual, firm, and regional covariates. Related Work: Existing research links commuting duration and spatial jobs-housing mismatch to reduced wellbeing, lower job engagement, and higher stress; other work frames resources provided by housing as buffers under the Job Demand-Resources model. Empirical approaches have largely relied on cross-sectional OLS regressions, correlations between commute time and mental health, and descriptive studies of employer-provided dormitories. Limitations of current approaches include (1) endogeneity and selection bias in housing choice not adequately addressed, (2) limited causal identification strategies and weak or absent instrumental variables, (3) scarce mediation analyses that unpack mechanisms such as labour intensity and work quality, (4) inadequate robustness checks across industry subgroups and urban policy contexts, and (5) lack of mixed-methods triangulation tying survey evidence to worker narratives. These gaps leave policy-relevant causal pathways and heterogeneous effects unresolved. Abstract: This pipeline operationalizes a mixed-method causal analysis to test whether job-housing balance reduces job burnout among migrant workers and to identify mediating mechanisms. The primary quantitative input is the 2018 China Labour Force Dynamic Survey (CLDS) subsample of employed adults (N≈2,758); qualitative triangulation uses semi-structured interviews from the Pearl River Delta (2023). The analytical strategy combines adjusted OLS, propensity-score matching, city fixed effects, instrumental-variable two-stage least squares (IV-2SLS) using urban dormitory prevalence measures, and causal mediation analysis with bias-corrected bootstrap to estimate direct and indirect effects via labour intensity and work quality. Planned heterogeneity tests compare manufacturing, service, and other sectors, and robustness checks exclude private-car owners and use alternative commute thresholds. The main contribution is a rigorously identified estimate of the causal effect of spatially balanced affordable housing on burnout and quantified mediation shares, informing evidence-based siting and subsidy policy for housing support targeted at vulnerable migrant workers. Experiments: Datasets: primary—2018 CLDS individual-level data (workers aged 16–65), sample N=2,758 after exclusions; qualitative—12 semi-structured interviews (Pearl River Delta, 2023) for mechanism validation. Outcome: job burnout index (sum of four MBI-derived items, higher=more burnout). Treatments: (A) dormitory residence (binary), (B) ordinal job-housing balance level: 4=dormitory, 3=commute<20min nondormitory, 2=commute 20–40min, 1=commute>40min. Mediators: labour intensity (binary: weekly hours>45), work quality (job satisfaction 1–5). Baselines: (1) OLS without mediators, (2) OLS with full control set (individual, enterprise, work, social capital, expectations), (3) propensity score matching (1:1, 1:4, caliper=0.05, kernel), (4) city fixed-effects OLS. Identification: IV-2SLS with two urban-level instruments—regional occupancy rate of labour dormitories and regional prevalence of job-housing balance—reporting first-stage F-statistics and underidentification tests. Mediation: causal mediation regressions and bias-corrected accelerated bootstrap (BCA) with 500–2000 resamples to estimate indirect effects and proportion mediated. Ablation studies: (a) compare dormitory proxy vs commute-threshold proxy, (b) remove labour intensity from regressions to observe coefficient shifts, (c) restrict sample by industry (manufacturing/service/other) and by private car ownership, (d) placebo test using an unrelated outcome (e.g., non-work leisure satisfaction) to assess specificity. Evaluation metrics: coefficient estimates, robust standard errors clustered at city level, p-values, 95% confidence intervals, ATT from PSM, first-stage F-stat, bootstrap CIs for mediation, and change-in-coefficient for suppression effects. Reporting: full regression tables, balance diagnostics for PSM, IV diagnostics, mediation effect sizes and % mediated, and qualitative vignettes aligned with quantitative pathways. Risk Factors and Limitations: Endogeneity: residual selection into dormitories or short commutes may persist despite IVs; instrument exclusion restriction may be violated by unobserved city-level factors correlated with burnout. Measurement error: self-reported commute time, weekly hours, and single-item job satisfaction may introduce attenuation bias. Cross-sectional design: temporal ordering between housing change, labour intensity, and burnout cannot be fully established, limiting causal claims about dynamics. External validity: interview sample focused on the Pearl River Delta and may not generalize to other regions or countries. Unobserved confounders: housing quality, employer coercion, shared-room crowding, and family circumstances are not fully measured. Mediation assumptions: causal mediation requires no unmeasured mediator–outcome confounding, an assumption that is difficult to verify with available data. Subgroup power: small subgroup samples (e.g., by industry or extreme commute categories) may lead to imprecise estimates. Computational/scalability limits: bootstrap mediation with many resamples and IV diagnostics require moderate compute but are feasible; however, extensions to panel or spatial models will increase complexity.
